speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity, which has to do with the latest issue by Canada Post of a philatelic description of postage stamps commemorating the 1976 Olympic games. In this one, as in other similar pamphlets issued earlier, Queen Elizabeth The Second of Canada is not mentioned. The reference to the opening of the Olympic games is, and I quote, "The Head of State normally declares the games open". This is another example of the way in which the Queen is being by-passed, and corresponds with some recent speeches made by the Prime Minister in which he refers to her as Queen of England, a gratuitous injustice to her, and contempt of the provisions of the Constitution and of Parliament, of which she is an integral part. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie):
That this House views with deep concern the manner in which the Trudeau government is endeavouring to undermine the position the Queen occupies as Queen of Canada by avoiding any mention of her.

Mr. Speaker, as I indicated when I made my statement giving the government's decision to extend our jurisdiction, the main element in the protection of our fisheries zone would be the consent and the acquiescence of other states which normally fish in what will be Canadian waters. In the absence of that consent, acceptance or acquiescence there would be very little effect derived from surveillance activities, as has been demonstrated in other cases. Because we have worked out, through bilateral negotiations with other countries, arrangements which will respect our jurisdiction, we believe that the surveillance role, while important, does not assume the same importance as the acquiescence of the other countries.
As I understand the arrangements under the system of extended jurisdiction, foreign vessels fishing in the Canadian economic zone would be there under licence from the government of Canada. It seems to me that the possibility of losing that licence should act as a very strong deterrent from infringing any of the Canadian regulations, and I believe it will be possible under that kind of regime to enforce Canadian jurisdiction. I should repeat what I have already said, that there has been at work within the government a task force preparing for the time when Canada will exercise its jurisdiction, and plans are being made to ensure that surveillance and enforcement can be carried out.

As my statement indicated, we will ensure that the 200-mile fishing zone is in place by January 1, 1977. It could happen earlier; probably it will not.

I hope these discussions will begin at an early date. We have not set a date at the moment but I hope the discussions will begin soon so that this aspect of our bilateral relations will not flare up into a matter of difficulty.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would point out to the hon. member that Canada's commitment in this area is already very high. I believe a statement will be made there. The right hon. member for Prince Albert has expressed, by way of a question of privilege, indignation at the remarks made yesterday by the right hon. Prime Minister. The right hon. Prime Minister has made a reply to that. Hon. members know that there is no process or procedure under which the Chair can permit a second intervention by the right hon. member for Prince Albert, and presumably a second intervention by the right hon. Prime Minister.
The matter is closed. It is for the Chair to decide. No motion has been put forward. The right hon. member for Prince Albert has called for either a clarification or a withdrawal of the statement made by the right hon. Prime Minister. It is not altogether certain whether or not this comes within the authority of the Chair under the provisions of questions of privilege, but in any case, the right hon. Prime Minister has indicated that he did not expect the matter would be taken seriously. In any case, it is entirely clear that the right hon. member for Prince Albert has not, in fact, contacted any member of the judiciary on this matter. This would seem to the Chair to close the question of privilege.

Mr. Speaker, earlier in the question period the hon. member for Toronto-Lake-shore made reference to his Bill C-242. You called him to order in the course of that, Mr. Speaker, but there was sufficient on the record before you called him to order to leave the impression that the official opposition, as a party, was opposed to this private member's bill. I think it is important to indicate to the House of Commons that that is not so. As I have said, the hon. member's bill is a private members' bill, and in that sense enjoys support on all sides of the House.
The House will recall that at the outset of the debate an attempt was made to draw out the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council and me, the House leader of the opposition, as if there had been some form or arrangement between us representing our parties in the private members' hour. I want to say that both of us studiously avoided that kind of involvement. It is interesting to note, as well-if it is any comfort to my good friend, the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore-that I spoke on second reading in support of the bill, and that those of our party who were on the committee which dealt with the bill spoke in favour of its principle. So I think there was general acceptance from all sides of the House to the priciple of the bill.
But I think it is important that we make it clear that private members' hour is just that, private members' hour, during which members of parliament can express their own personal views on the matters discussed. I want to make it extremely clear, especially to the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore, who I know has laboured for a long period of time on this matter, that our party is not opposed to the principle set forth in this bill, and in fact a careful reading of the committee's hearings will indicate that that is so.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the budget there are a number of measures which deserve discussion. I will devote a few minutes to talking about two aspects of the budget. One has to do with a proposed measure with regard to unemployment insurance, and the other has to do with the budget measures relating to energy conservation, and in particular to those which provide incentives for the development of alternative forms of energy.
With regard to unemployment insurance, the question which comes to mind and which is probably in the minds of those who are interested in this issue is really this: How many weeks of contribution are considered to be fair, in a social security program like unemployment insurance, before qualifying for benefits? It seems to me that the issue boils down to that basic question. If we consider other programs of a similar nature-for example, workmen's compensation, medicare and hospital insurance-we will find that in most of those programs one can become eligible for protection from the moment one starts contributing to those systems.
In other words, to the best of my knowledge there is no qualifying period for coverage; a person is covered from the moment he starts contributing. This is true in the public sector for programs of the kind I have mentioned, and it is also true in the private sector. If a person starts paying premiums for home insurance, life insurance, or any other form of insurance, for that matter, he is covered from the moment he starts paying into the scheme. Therefore, it is natural to conclude-at least, it is to me-that under the unemployment insurance scheme it is desirable to strive for a system whereby a person can qualify for coverage from the moment he joins, because that is the pattern and the criterion which has been applied to other insurance schemes both in the private and public sectors.
If we ask the proponents of 12 weeks, 16 weeks or more to give a reasoning for that period of time before qualifying, we will notice that it is very difficult, even with the best of intentions, for them to come forward with rationale for that. I cannot provide the rationale for 8 weeks either, but if I were asked what we as a government should strive for over a period of time, my answer would be that it should be something which will take us in a direction opposite to the proposal in this budget, namely, toward lowering, rather than increasing, the number of weeks required to qualify for unemployment insurance.
I know it is very popular at the present time in this country to be tough with regard to unemployment insurance. I know there is much support for the idea of increasing the number of weeks. However, I do not share that view, because I think we have in unemployment insurance a good social program which protects people, particularly in those areas of the country where employment is seasonal and the availability of jobs is very limited. Those areas are away from large industrial centres and include areas such as New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, P.E.I., parts of Quebec, northern Ontario and virtually all the areas of the country which benefit at present from our regional economic expansion programs.
I may be wrong, but I have noticed-despite the speech made by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) who, on behalf of the Conservative party, supported the
The Budget-Mr. Caccia
increase in the number of weeks-a certain nervousness in Conservative ranks as expressed in questions asked by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) on May 27 and by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Howie) on June 7. If that impression is correct, I can well understand that nervousness because some areas of this country will be seriously affected by the change in the number of weeks from 8 to 12 as proposed in this budget.
It seems to me that when a person becomes unemployed, that person becomes unemployed for reasons beyond his or her control. A good social security measure, therefore, should be available at the earliest possible time-in the shortest number of weeks that the social security system can offer. I am not so impressed by arguments that are based on the question of abuse. It is very easy to make a charge of abuse, but to the question of where the abuse occurs the answer rarely comes forth.
It must be kept in mind-and this seems to be forgotten by those who are criticizing the unemployment insurance policy-that if a person quits his or her job without reason, that person goes without benefits for six full weeks. That is a pretty long time to be without benefits, Mr. Speaker. There seems to be an impression that you qualify for unemployment insurance the moment you quit, or a week or two after. That is not so. If you quit without reason, you go six weeks without benefits. No one in his right mind would want to abandon a job with the knowledge that the social security system, in this case unemployment insurance, will not be forthcoming in less than a month and a half.
I would, therefore, urge the government to reconsider this measure in the budget and to stick with the eight weeks. It is a good measure. As the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) said, our unemployment insurance system is one of the best in the world. We should not be ashamed of it or retreat from it; we should be very proud of it. If the government does not find it possible to reconsider this measure for the whole country, I would suggest, as an alternative, that we retain the eight-week period of contributions before benefits are payable in those regions of Canada presently benefiting from regional economic expansion. I would urge that compromise at least.
I should like to devote the little time I have left to another aspect of the budget, Mr. Speaker, for which I would like to congratulate the government and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald). I refer to the measure that was announced on May 26 concerning energy conservation. In particular, I refer to the two-year tax write-off that is extended to cover equipment enabling industrial wastes to be used as a fuel source and industrial equipment that produces energy from municipal waste. In addition to that, the federal sales tax is removed from items which contribute to energy conservation or contribute to the development of alternative forms of energy, including solar furnaces and heating panels, wind-powered generating equipment and heat pumps.
Before I go on, Mr. Speaker, I should like to pay tribute to the work done in this area over the years, when it was rather like crying in the desert, by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton). For years he

June 9, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Gillies
has appealed for better use of wind energy in the part of the country from which he comes. Now we have come to the crunch. We have reached a point in history when it is quite clear to us that we will run out of non-renewable resources. The government's measure reflects concern and foresight in anticipation of things to come.
The Globe and Mail of June 8 published a report which read in part:
A background study prepared for the federal government estimates that renewable energy sources could provide anywhere from 2 per cent to 4 per cent of the country's total energy requirements by 1990.
It went on to say that the study reports that by the year 2020 the percentage could rise to 20 per cent of energy needs. Mr. Speaker, I am more optimistic than that, although I cannot base my optimism on any scientific knowledge. I think that at present we are badly underestimating the potential of the sun as an energy source. What concerns me is the fact that when we make $122 million available for research and development for this fiscal year, according to my calculations only 2.2 per cent of that is available for research in the renewable energy field, namely, sun, wind and tidal. I think this is an alarmingly low percentage. If we cannot increase the total amount, I would at least urge the government to review the percentage or the slice that is allocated from the research and development total fund and give much greater emphasis to research in the field of renewable energy.
As things stand at the moment, of the $122 million allocated for research and development, 8 'A per cent is for research on conservation, 10 per cent for oil and gas, 4.5 per cent for coal, almost 70 per cent for nuclear, 5V4 per cent for transportation and transmission, and only 2.2 per cent for renewable resources. In light of the very important decision embodied in the budget respecting energy conservation and incentives for the discovery and implementation of new sources of energy, I think it is imperative that we give much greater impetus to research in the field of renewable energy resources.
It seems to me that the next step will lead to the creation of a Canadian industry based on Canadian technology in the field of solar energy and, following that, the creation of industries and jobs. Then would come the development of a market at home and with countries which have similar climatic conditions to ours or, indeed, even different climatic conditions. There is an opportunity at hand, and I am certain we have the knowledge if we have the political will to move in that direction with greater speed and determination than the figures would seem to indicate.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to commence my remarks this afternoon by congratulating the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) for the brilliant speech he delivered last night on the budget. It was a speech full of original ideas and observations which, if they were followed by the government, would put this country in better shape than it is today.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not intend to spend much time this afternoon talking about the specific deficiencies of this budget. Both inside and outside this House, the lack of any
(Mr. Caccia.]
direction in the budget, the inability of the government to decide what it is trying to do, the loss of faith which is shown in this nation as perceived by an almost pathetic suggestions that Canada's economic destiny is controlled by foreign forces, has been commented upon by newspaper editorials and reporters very, very widely. To me, other than the technical deficiencies in the analysis and in the proposals, both in terms of economic policy-making and the government's attitude toward energy, the most disturbing aspects of this stand-pat budget, as it has been called, is that the government has so little confidence in this great nation that it can suggest at this time that what we need is a stand-pat budget when we have inflation at an annual rate of 9 per cent and unemployment at a seasonally adjusted rate of 7.4 per cent, which means that 760,000 Canadians are out of work.
The government is apparently accepting this incredibly poor economic performance and literally believes, in spite of the great resources of this country, in spite of the quality of the labour force, in spite of the fact that we have been isolated from the oil crisis created by the OPEC countries, in spite of an abundant agricultural sector, that Canada should have a slower rate of economic recovery than many other countries of the world, much slower than that of our major trading partner, the United States, and that average economic performance vis-a-vis other countries is satisfactory.
Why is there so little vision in this budget? Why, when there are such opportunities and potentials for creating a veritable Utopia in Canada, has the government turned its back on the people in the country by offering nothing? Do we not have one of the greatest opportunities of any people anywhere for creative development of techniques to bring oil from tar sands? Do we not have an overwhelming opportunity to find out new ways for operating in northern areas, new ways which could be useful for all other countries with Arctic resources? Are we not, perhaps, on the brink of one of the most exciting and far-reaching national ventures-one unparallelled since the building of the great cross-country railroads at the end of the nineteenth century-with the possible construction of pipelines from the northern resource areas?
Do we not have the great challenge of making the cities more livable and housing more available? Where is the thrust toward public transport, the ultimate aid in conservation, if not only of energy but of the urban environment? Where is the policy to encourage dispersion of industry so that we can have imaginative and controlled development of urban regions? Where is the program to really deal with structural unemployment and regional disparities? Where is the imagination that links what we could be with what we are? Where is the potentiality for taking us from underutilization of our resources to full use, for the benefit of all?
How can we accept, in the face of what we could be doing in this nation, an attitude that 7.4 per cent of the labour force unemployed, and a growth rate of less than 5 per cent, is acceptable? Again I ask, what has happened? Where is the vision? Where is the effort to rise to the opportunity? This tone of defeatism in the budget, in this
June 9, 1976

land of potentiality, surely must be disturbing-indeed distressing-to every Canadian.
The budget reflects, of course, the tone and attitude of the government, a tone and attitude that there are only problems, not opportunities; that Canadians are tired and weary; that our horizons have narrowed; that we cannot be better than we are, cannot strive to influence and shape our own destiny; that we are caught in the throes of worldwide events; that we must surrender our dreams and aspirations; that we must look for less, not more; that we cannot show the way. How wrong this is. What a misreading it is of what Canadians want from a government. What a reflection it is of a government that has been in power too long, that is tired, worn-out, unimaginative and uninspiring.
A budget is, of course, a technical document as well as a statement of economic aspirations of the government and, therefore, the country. The economic aspirations of this government are to hope for a gradual decline in inflation from its current level of 9 per cent to 4 per cent in 1978, an aspiration for performance 100 per cent less than the aspirations of the United States government which is looking for a 2 per cent inflation rate at the end of 1977.
The government is also looking for a gradual decline of unemployment with the oft-repeated suggestion that the actual unemployment rate in Canada will decline when the rest of the world recovers. This analysis, or premise, concerning what happens in the rest of the world apparently has become the cornerstone of economic policy-making of this government. It was the explanation used by the former minister of finance for his inability to turn the Canadian economy around. He will undoubtedly be remembered as the most incompetent and, finally, least courageous minister of finance this country has ever had. And it is the explanation now used by the present minister. I can only conclude that it is the basic and unswerving position of the officials of the Department of Finance.
It is this type of thinking which is destructive for the nation, because it is the ultimate cop-out for doing nothing on the domestic scene and, significantly, it also permits the abdication of careful analysis of alternatives and assessment of past performances to see if, in fact, we could have done better. When everything is determined by something beyond your control, the need for accountability of performance is removed.
No one would argue that Canada is not a part of the global economy, and a significant part. No one would argue that Canadian economic performance is unaffected by what happens in other countries. But where great issue can be taken with the minister and his advisers is that they believe Canada can take no action on its own to mitigate the impact of changes in the world economy on the Canadian economy; or, indeed, that Canada can take no actions which can in fact influence the world economy. We are not spectators in the world; we are participants. But we can influence events in the world economy, just as we can influence the impact of world events on the Canadian economy. By knowing and analysing what is happening in the world, we can adopt policies to channel the consequences of such events in Canada's interest. To suggest that we can do nothing is a surrender of responsibility and
The Budget-Mr. Gillies
ought to, and will, lead to surrender of the right to govern much longer by the party now in power.
The general apathetic, helpless approach to budget-market has been reinforced in recent years by an increasing emphasis on the part of the government on the use of broad or macroeconomic tools in preparation of the budget. While it is true that since the work of Lord Keynes in the 1930s there has been recognition of the fact that the levels of expenditures and revenues by government can greatly influence the direction of economic activity in the nation, during the past few years in Canadian budget-making there has been so much emphasis on the broad forces that influence the economy that it has been forgotten, or indeed underemphasized, that the way in which these broad forces are created is as important as their size. This retreat from traditional classical analysis has led to gross errors in the management of the Canadian economy.
Moreover, it is apparent that much less is known about the impact of gross changes in the economy than was believed only a decade ago. One does not hear much today about "fine-tuning" the economy, one of the catch phrases of the early seventies. The fact is that economists, certainly not the economists advising this government, simply do not know what impact spending, taxing and other proposals will have on the economy. The effects anticipated from specific action in periods of less competition, inflationary expectations and huge government intervention in the economy are simply, at this stage in the development of economic knowledge, unknown and unpredictable -Yet in spite of all the evidence that they do not know what they are doing, evidence supported by the record of past performance, the minister insists on bringing in a budget based on the same type of analysis at that of his predecessors. Unfortunately, it will have the same consequences for the Canadian people.
Look at some of the paradoxes. The governor of the Bank of Canada argues that it is necessary to have rapid increases in the money supply to keep interest rates down. So Canada has had a money supply increase at an unprecedented level and has, not what we were told we would get, low interest rates, but the highest interest rates in its history. In the United States, the federal reserve system has kept its rate of increase in the money supply low and interest rates are substantially lower in that country than in Canada. Clearly, it is not the rate of increase in the money supply but other factors which are establishing interest rates: But our Canadian officials do not seem to understand this simple proposition.
Consider the fact, implicit in the remarks of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) about his budget, that his officials are still talking about a trade-off in unemployment and inflation. Yet the facts are clear. We have not had in this country a substantial change in the rate of inflation as unemployment has risen. The trade-off in any meaningful sense, within any acceptable limits, simply does not exist. The facts appear, rather, to support the proposition that unemployment is created by increasing inflation and that both rise together. The policy-making is based on the false premise of the trade-off. So it is no wonder that the economic performance in Canada, in spite of the enormous advantages inherent within this nation, is so poor. Economic policy-making here is based upon a

June 9, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Gillies
theory of economy which is simply not appropriate for the time. As long as this error persists, we will have poor economic performance.
The greatest example, and the one with possibly the most extreme consequences of the error of concentrating on broad aspects of the economy instead of looking with great care at specific sectors, can be seen in the way in which the energy sector of this nation has been mishandled by the present government for the past few years. The incompetence, which can almost be labelled as scandalous, of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources and the National Energy Board in forecasting Canada's energy resources has been commented on many times. Today it is simply unbelievable that within this decade responsible members of the government were stating that we had endless supplies of oil and natural gas for our own needs, that we could export unlimited amounts to our neighbour, and yet next year we will probably be a net importer of oil.
It is truly unthinkable that as recently as three years ago the government had a taxing policy that literally discouraged exploration and development. It is again almost unbelievable that through the past years the government has not worked out a meaningful process for discussing and resolving energy questions which involve different jurisprudences. The fact is that even today we do not have a carefully thought-through program for conservation and development of alternative energy supplies, and yet we know that without energy great problems are ahead of us.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) spoke in the budget debate. I read his remarks with care. Most of what he said had been put forth before, and with some of it I agree. The time is long past, however, since Canada has needed an appropriate tax regime that would encourage exploration and development. The feeble steps that the government are taking in this direction are welcome, but not nearly enough. The bold imagination necessary to move effectively in the tar sands, in the north, across this entire continent, are lacking. Nothing is done for the mining industry which through the years has been one of the most important elements in the development of the Canadian economy.
What is most startling, however, and indicative of what is wrong in the way the government is approaching the problems of the nation is that the minister in his speech said very little about energy in relation to the Canadian balance of payments. I make this point because Canada's balance of payments difficulties are going to have a profound effect on every Canadian in the course of the next few years, and many of the problems are created because of our inability to deal with energy. If a solution had been found for our energy needs, a solution which would shift reliance from imports and such a high volume of domestic consumption of oil and natural gas to other sources, then our balance of payments problems would be less threatening. In 1985, the Economic Council of Canada predicts, 38 per cent of the deficit in the balance of payments will be from petroleum products-something which indeed is scandalous, given our resource base.
It is not helpful, however, to discuss the balance of payment problems in a vacuum. It is a product of neglect
of various segments of the Canadian economy, each one of which should have been dealt with specifically in the budget and by policy through the years. Again, this is one of the prices that has been paid for so much emphasis on broad policy-making. The neglect of the elements which in the last analysis are influenced by that policy, and indeed how they react in the long-run, determines whether or not such broad policies will, in fact, work.
What are the Canadian balance of payments problems, and why are they so serious for the Canadian economy? In the most simplistic sense, the base of the problem is simply that Canada is buying far more from other countries- buying, that is, services, payments for capital, and everything else-than she is selling to all other countries in the world. Indeed, Canada had a deficit, in this sense, of $5.1 billion in 1975. Since things that are purchased have to be paid for, Canada borrowed $4.7 billion in 1975 to help make up the difference. So in this period when the government is saying it is the policy to lessen foreign ownership in Canada, we are in fact faced with an economic situation which simply requires that foreign investment increases, unless we do something about it.
If we do not want to borrow, the only other thing that can happen is that the Canadian dollar can be devalued and devalued, it will be if the present situation continues. But what does this mean? Fundamentally, it means that Canadian imports will be more expensive, and that has to mean strong inflationary pressures on the Canadian economy. Although, because it is the conventional wisdom of the Minister of Finance and his officials to believe that this will increase exports because the dollar will be cheaper, the recent work of Professor Mundell of Columbia University suggests this is not true, and the evidence of the past few years supports him.
The fact is that the rise in the price of imports, and the inflation which this rise in price creates, has meant that devaluation has led, in every country he has studied, to a rise in costs to such an extent that it more than offsets the advantages of the cheaper currency. What country in the world has had the most continuous devaluation of their currency? Great Britain. And it has had the longest period of balance of payments problems. What country has had no balance of payments problems and has maintained high levels of exports? Germany. And it has not had a continuous pattern of devaluation.
It is a myth to think that devaluation will solve the balance of payments problems. It will not. It will simply add to inflation and exacerbate the difficulties. If the government does not recognize this, and if it is not prepared to see the entire Canadian economy owned by non-Canadians, it must totally revamp its economic policies or we will never get out of the inflation-unemployment dilemma which we are now experiencing.
What has to be done? We need to cut back on exports where it is possible to do so; not through tariffs or restrictive trade practices, but where we can substitute domestic production for imports on an economic basis. Certainly, this means a crash program in energy development, a program to move the tar sands ahead on a priority basis, a program to generate energy from alternative sources, the tides, the wind, the sun and nuclear power properly safeguarded. The minuscule approach to this effort indicated

June 9, 1976

by this budget clearly shows the government has no realization of the scope and implications of the change in Canada from an exporter of energy to an importer, implications for the balance of payments and the rest of the economy.
Second, we must increase our exports, not through devaluation, because devaluation will not work, but by making the areas in which Canada has a world advantage more competitive and more productive. Tax policy must be directed at stimulating productivity, at developing our mineral resources, at improving our forest industries and keeping our agricultural sector one of the most competitive and efficient in the world. The Economic Council of Canada is absolutely correct in stating that we have to move away, in our policy, from programs that put us in direct competition with Hong Kong, Taiwan and other Far-Eastern countries which are labour-intensive. We have to strengthen our industries through tax treatment, incentive programs and general support where we have some advantage. Our future is based on resources and advanced technology and we must build our policies to strengthen these areas.
The current account in trade has been in deficit in seven of the past ten years. Despite the wishful thinking of the government that this problem will go away as the world economy recovers, it will not. Canadian export trade developed in the late fifties and over the sixties because of the Kennedy Round, Viet Nam, the auto pact and other special circumstances. It is all changing. The world is developing into trading blocs and Canada is not in one of them. The Kennedy Round approach is being replaced by bilateral negotiations and commodities, and it is certain that the trading patterns of the 1950s and 1960s will not be repeated. The automobile may be on the decline in this energy-short society, so if Canada is to prosper through trade it must have new policies and be more competitive.
Therefore, this budget deserves all the condemnation that it has had from Canadians from coast to coast. It lacks vision of what this country can be, and therefore has no policies for the long-run approach to the fulfilment of the nation's potentialities. It continues to emphasize broad-gauged fiscal and monetary policies which, important as they are, are less reliable for guiding the economy because no one knows what the results of such policies will be in an inflationary, government-dominated nation. It neglects the traditional task of a budget of producing policies and programs for specific sectors of the economy which must be supported if inflation and unemployment are to be reduced. It is based upon an out-moded and patently incorrect analysis of the manner in which an economy operates. It neglects to come to grips with the most significant approaching economic problem Canada is facing-the enormous deficits in our buying and selling relationships with the rest of the world.
In studying this budget and the philosophy, economic analysis and confidence in Canada which lies behind its formulation, Canadians can only conclude that the present government is worn-out, tired, incompetent and incapable of providing the leadership which a nation with the great opportunity and potentiality of Canada clearly deserves to have.
The Budget-Mr. Chretien

Mr. Speaker, before I go further I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) on his presentation. He talked in a very commendable way about the budget, expressing his views upon it and upon what should be done.
I was surprised to hear him speak as he did about the devaluation of the Canadian dollar. As he knows, there are many articles being written at this time suggesting that we should weaken the value of the Canadian dollar in relation to the American dollar-it is now two or three points above the U.S. valuation. I am glad to note that the hon. member recognizes that there are a lot of people in Canada who say that if we want to improve our export position, we ought to have a kind of devaluation. I will pass the hon. member's views on to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald). At least the hon. member for Don Valley is very happy with the healthy situation of the Canadian dollar at the present time and he does not want to change it. It is a fact of life. I was surprised to hear his condemnation of the government at the end of his speech, to the effect that it was a tired, old government, and so on. I do not feel tired at all.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As I say, I am happy to know there is one member who is in accord with this particular aspect of Canadian fiscal and monetary policy to the extent that the Canadian dollar should be, not at par or below the value of the American dollar but that it should be a healthier dollar.
I have notes today. Usually I provoke a lot of controversy when I speak, so on this occasion I have written down the observations I intend to make. In rising today to participate in the budget debate, I would like to discuss two aspects of my responsibility as President of the Treasury Board. First, I will speak about government spending and then I will turn to the subject of the official languages policy.
Government spending is a matter which has been receiving much attention for a long time. It is right that it should receive a lot of attention because it is very important. The trouble is that it is also very complicated, and many of those who may have much to say on the subject have not taken the trouble to learn enough to understand it. As a result, a great deal of criticism people hear is misinformed. It is not forgivable for a large segment of the opposition to be so wrong-headed in talking about government expenditures when they should be giving leadership through informed criticism. But how can they give leadership when they stand paralysed in an attempted acrobatic effort to move in three directions at the same time? They advocate cutting government expenditures in total, but are critical of cutting expenditures in any particular area. In a third dimension, they favour a whole lot of new ideas which involve expenditure. Let me touch on a few points to entertain these hon. members as they stand in their fixed position.
First, let us consider the question of the growth of expenditures. This is usually looked at in terms of current

The Budget-Mr. Chretien
dollars discounting the effects of the use in prices. In those terms, total outlays, both budgetary and non-budgetary, rose 25 per cent in 1973-74, 28 per cent in 1974-75, and according to necessarily preliminary figures presented in the budget, by 18 per cent in 1975-76. But in terms of constant dollars, with the effect of price increases removed through a deflator, the actual rise in the years I have mentioned was 15 per cent in 1972-73, 15 per cent in 1973-74, 13 per cent in 1974-75, and 8 per cent in 1975-76-a different story, one of persistent decline. If we achieve our aim of staying under a ceiling of 14 per cent growth in 1976-77, price effects included, the growth in real terms will be no more than 5 per cent, maintaining the decline.
As hon. members know, our commitment to the future is that the trend of growth in expenditures by all levels of government will not exceed to trend of growth in the gross national product. This is a collective responsibility which the provinces and municipalities must share if it is to be discharged. I have shown in the record of decline just set out that we can be expected to do our part.
The word "trend" is significant. No government worth electing would bind itself to an automatic formula. Should the economy require assistance through added expenditures from time to time, the assistance must be given. Recent history offers a pertinent case in point. There is little doubt that the performance of the Canadian economy during the recent period of slow growth was assisted by the fact that federal expenditures remained at a high level. We avoided the decline in GNP which our neighbour suffered.
I maintain that our advanced social welfare structure, put in place by a series of Liberal governments, had much to do with this favourable outcome. The collection of programs which make up this structure has, as its primary purpose, the relieving of hardship among those who are the beneficiaries. But the indirect, cumulative effect is to maintain the purchasing power of the domestic economy in the face of downward pressures. So what we intend to do, by and large, is to hold expenditure growth over the medium and long term to the trend of the GNP. But we will depart from that trend when it is the right thing to do.
There is another general aspect of government expenditures which is analogous to the welfare aspect and which appears to go unnoticed. A large part of what is spent is in the nature of investment. Every year hundreds of millions of dollars are disbursed in budgetary outlays for capital acquisitions. The convention of the government accounts is to write off these outlays in the year they occur. The balance-sheet of Canada contains an almost quaint entry of one dollar to represent the value of all these budgetary investments from all the years this country has been in existence. That is a very big dollar. Business and commercial practice would show, in similar circumstances, an entry for billions of dollars, as well it might. The airports, the wharves, the roads, the postal terminals are in their own way as productive facilities as the factories and stores which weigh heavily in valuations of the commercial sector.
I have mentioned on other occasions that after you subtract transfer payments to other governments and to
individuals, and after you subtract subsidies to transportation, research and the like, and after you subtract public debt charges, you are left with a few percentage points of the total. These few percentage points include all the budgetary capital investments I have been talking about.
On the non-budgetary side, productive investment is much more marked. Here, our accounting practice is a little close to the commercial. The public accounts for 1974-75 show $1,831 million as a return to the government on its investments. These investments include, very prominently, the mortgage funds provided to CMHC to assist housing, the funds given to the Export Development Corporation to promote export, those given to the Farm Credit Corporation to assist agriculture, the Northern Canada Power Commission to support northern development, and much more.
What I have been trying to counteract here is the false impression created by so many who wave around the big figures of total expenditures in a way that hides the beneficial effect. The subject of the beneficial effect, through transfers to all segments of our society, I hope I have covered often enough before. These investment aspects are not mentioned frequently enough.
I really must deal, now, with the remarks made the other day by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens). To say the nice things first, his remarks do serve some purpose in that they illustrate what I meant about uninformed criticism. I have not the time to reply to everything he said, so I will content myself with some of the juicier morsels. He started with the Post Office, about a difference between the 1975-76 expenditures figures for that department as forecast in the main estimates and as reported in the budget papers. Surely the hon. member must know by now that the main estimates are compiled in the December preceding the start of the fiscal year on the basis of departmental submissions received around the end of October. One figure is a forecast made some months before the year ends, and the other is a figure reported after the year ends. He must also be aware, if he was around, that there was a postal strike last year, a little incident that lasted for many, many weeks.

May we all give fervent thanks that the finances of this country are not in such hands. Perhaps

now, Mr. Speaker, I can turn to my other preoccupation for today.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to deal now with the government program on official languages. As you know, the cost of such programs gives rise to many comments, particularly because of the present restriction period. However, from the outset the consideration of all those linguistic matters must be placed in its real context.
As for any other government program, the funds allocated to the official language program are now subject to the strictest assessment. In the light of available data, the government estimates will have to spend about $310 million on those linguistic programs during the current fiscal year. This represents .8 of 1 per cent of the government overall spending which, according to the estimates, will be around $42 billion.
If we compare the cost of the official language programs with those of other sectors, we see that the linguistic programs require less money than the military equipment needed for national defence: $322 million. The same goes for the manpower rehabilitation and training program: $530 million.

This is one of the arguments they use. They think these are consulting firms.

As for the program concerning the native people of Canada, their budget of $605 million is almost double the total budget for official languages.
Out of the total projections of $310 million, 43 per cent or approximately $135 million are included in transfers for financing provincial programs of second language education. The amount of $135 million is spent and transferred to provincial governments, to Quebec for teaching English as well as outside Quebec for teaching French. In other words, the government has already agreed to the wishes expressed by the Commissioner of Official Languages and others that it would be more profitable to invest in young people attending school.
Moreover, $39 million were assigned to the bilingual program for military personnel in order that a national service of the scope of the Canadian Armed Forces can, within the country and abroad, reflect the bilingualism of Canada.
Regarding expenditures on programs for Canadian civil servants, these will reach $137 million, approximately half the subsidies to be paid to milk producers. That figure includes the cost of language training for civil servants, that of translation services for all documents, of course translation services for the House of Commons, and the budget of the Commissioner of Official Languages and also the operation costs incurred by my department under vote 15, that is the salaries of civil servants absent from work to follow language courses. The total is $137 million. All translation services at the House of Commons-

There have been reservations concerning the linguistic designation of jobs within the Public Service of Canada and the language training program for civil servants. It has been implied for example that the identification of too many bilingual jobs would of necessity entail a lack of unilingual ones. However, any evaluation of that particular aspect of the program must adhere strictly to the original aims and criteria followed in the identification of language requirements for each job.
Under the Official Languages Act, government policies and programs are intended firstly to ensure that members of the Canadian community can communicate with and be served by federal bodies and departments in their own official language. The second objective is to make available to public servants every opportunity to work in the official language of their choice.
Procedures which were used to identify the linguistic requirements for various positions, while taking into consideration previous objectives, were described in the text of the resolution adopted in June 1973 by all parties represented in the House of Commons. The system used to identify the requirements for positions were not designed as if the situation would never change. On the contrary, it was meant to adapt to any situation which could arise and to promote the development of the official languages whenever it was desirable. I should point out in that respect that the resolution on official languages also included provisions for the increasing use of French within the confines of the merit principle, thus involving both francophone and anglophone communities in the federal administration process. The positions have therefore been identified to meet not only immediate needs, but also future requirements of the linguistic development of the public service.
As I already announced publicly, the Treasury Board, in cooperation with federal agencies and departments, will undertake the systematic review of linguistic requirements of all federal positions. If, in the light of the data collected during this review, we have to recognize that too many bilingual positions have been identified within the federal administrations, we shall not hesitate to take the required action.
In November 1974, I announced in the House that the government had decided to commission some experts to study linguistic training programs in the public service. The government has just received the thick report prepared by this study group, and it is now being translated and printed. We hope to make it public as soon as possible.
I would like to take this opportunity to express on behalf of the government my gratefulness to Mr. Gilles Bibeau of the University of Montreal who was asked to direct this important study. I would like to tell him once again that the government will study closely his evaluation and recommendations.
There is no doubt that the transformation of the Public Service of Canada into a functionally bilingual institution at an acceptable but fair cost is an enormous task. The concept of linguistic planning is in itself revolutionary and until now, no other country in the world has undertaken such a wide linguistic training program for adults.

In concluding, I could not overemphasize the importance of another dimension of official languages, because it would be wrong to reduce them to a simple linguistic matter. If through that linguistic reform we want to achieve a civil service that provides services suited to the needs of the Canadian public on the one hand and, on the other hand, a hospitable working climate for the civil servant, the Public Service of Canada will have to become aware of and sensitive to the culture dimension. In other words, when it comes to a decision likely to affect the whole of this country, it is important for those who participate in the decision-making process to seek to understand and respect provincial variables. In short, we must pursue

Civil servants of both linguistic groups will be able to work together toward common goals using their own language and drawing from their respective cultural values while at the same time appreciating to their full value and respecting those of others.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is very important at this moment to thank everyone in the various departments in Ottawa for their great understanding of the government's policy in this respect. I think we have made a lot of progress. There is much good will, and this should be emphasized more often because I know that in my department this has been a great experience. As I have said in my speech, everyone uses his own language at meetings when we have to make decisions. This is of great satisfaction even to people who sometimes appear to object the most to this policy.
It is sometimes said that we do not provide sufficient opportunity for those who have learned the French language, to use it. Some people say that not enough French is spoken in Ottawa. I must tell hon. members that I have been a member of the House since 1963, and in my view the situation now is completely different. Sometimes when we have technical discussions in my department I prefer to use my native language. I speak in French, which my officials understand, and they reply in English. This is the kind of attitude that is being developed and one which is gratifying to both sides.
In my view, too many people tend to raise the problems and not talk about the results. The other day I heard someone complain that some people claim they use French only 9 per cent or 10 per cent of the time. I refer here to English people who have learned French. Some Englishspeaking officials in Ottawa have learned French and use it only 10 per cent of the time, and yet this is a revolution, a revolution in the right direction. I think we have gained from those exchanges.
Of course there are many problems, but I think that not enough people speak about the real progress that has been achieved, the understanding between people and their willingness to understand each other. We should not try to put into perspective only the problems, because there will always be problems. I see, after talking with members on both sides of the House and from all parties, that they want this policy to be a success. This will not take place overnight, but I think every one of us should look at the problem realistically and not forget the good progress we have made in the last ten years in Canada in this respect. The other day I was in British Columbia and some people came up to me to talk about this policy, people who want to be part of the fabric of this nation, who want to have access to the two greatest western cultures, the French and the English. There are other components-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) must have put a lot of time and effort into the drafting of this budget. It is obvious that this has not been a hasty effort or one lacking in ingenuity, either. It took an awful lot of planning, enterprise and expertise to prepare a budget that does not contain a single, solitary item that should have been in the budget. In fact, it is such a sterile and useless document that the Minister of Finance might have used his time to better advantage, possibly rounding up some money with which to buy long-range patrol aircraft for the Canadian armed forces. There are so many things missing from this budget that it might become famous as the case of the missing budget. It might have to share billing with Keith Spicer's famous annual reports on the failure of bilingualism in the public service, or that infamous volume of instructions on how to tender for contracts at the nation's federal airports.
Because of its shortcomings, this budget is guaranteed a place in history, the history of "nothing" budgets, "nothing" reports and "nothing" programs, because there is not a program in it. It was inspired and inaugurated by the Liberal aggregation across the floor. It is not surprising that the advisers of the Minister of Finance disagreed with him as to what kind of budget this is. The finance minister said that it is slightly stimulative and mildly expansionary. His economic advisers are reported to have described the budget as mildly restrictive. Surely, a minister responsible for approving and tabling national budgets should know the difference between expansionary and restrictive policies; at least that is what I hope.
Things do not change much from day to day around here in the life of this Trudeau government. It staggers along in disarray and chaos. The situation has become so bad that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his cabinet are now unable to confront the confusion, corruption, hypocrisy and ineptitude of his administration. The multi-million dollar loss incurred by either one of his two ministers, or both, in the ill-fated Lockheed deal is the latest albatross around the neck of the Trudeau government, and the best thing the Prime Minister could do would be to sack both the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) and the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer). The government's policies are damaging our economy, or what is left of it.
We had the dubious distinction last Thursday afternoon of being the spectators of stormy scenes here on the Hill, brought about by the demonstration of the Quebec milk producers. That demonstration proved to be quite impressive. I can appreciate their milk marketing problem because I come from a farm background. I have milked cows and helped produce milk at ridiculously low prices in the past, and I have witnessed milk surpluses in my area as well as nationally. Nevertheless, I cannot condone the
damage done to public property by a small minority of the Quebec milk producers. If this deliberate vandalism does not stop, the government should ban all demonstrations on the upper concourse in front of the Peace Tower and permit demonstrations on the lower level of the front lawn only. Persons and property must be protected. That is the first duty of the government. But the Prime Minister can blame himself and his own policies to a great degree for the terrible state of general insolvency in the dairy industry in Canada today.
The Prime Minister has been the chief abettor of the main grievance of the Quebec dairy farmers, namely, the accumulated surplus milk products and the lack of market for this surplus. I want the House to pay special attention to the following: The Prime Minister's importing this year of 50 million pounds of cheese, much of it from the European Common Market, which is part of his much vaunted contractual link with that group of nations, only contributes to our own surplus. This represents about 500 million pounds of milk and costs our producers an additional $3.6 million over and above our current surpluses. This import item of cheese was one of the chief points of protest raised by the Quebec milk producers.
One of the statements made by the finance minister on budget night sticks in my mind and worries me, but I think it was the closest the minister has ever come to levelling with us. He said: "The outlook for 1977 is, of course, much more uncertain at this time." Every finance minister since the present government took office could say, and in many cases did, that the coming fiscal year looked uncertain. We have lived for a long time in that atmosphere of uncertainty-too long-and it shows up in everything we see when we summon the nerve to look around us.
I just have time to look in one more direction at present. We should consider our manufacturing industry and certain parts of it. The budget does nothing for our manufacturers, our secondary industry and especially for the textile industry. The Canadian textile industry, in all its facets, is in deep trouble and severely depressed because of our damaging imports of vast quantities of low-cost offshore products. I received a protest from Celanese Canada Limited, the owner and operator of a large plant at Mill-haven in my constituency of Frontenac-Lennox and Addington. I want to put that protest on the record. I have a letter here from Celanese Canada dated May 17 which reads in part as follows:
Dear Mr. Alkenbrack,
Further to my letter of April 15th, the polyester yarn business continues to be severely depressed. You may have noticed since that our competitor, DuPont, has deferred the opening of a new plant at Coteau-du-Lac, Quebec.
We have now found it necessary to cut back production further at our Millhaven, Ontario plant. This entails the lay-off of an additional 94 employees, bringing to 465 the total number of jobs lost this year in the Company's polyester filament yarn operations in Ontario.
I also received a resolution from the county of Lennox and Addington. The county government is so concerned about this that it sent this resolution to me, to many other elected representatives in this House and in the provincial government in Toronto. The county government goes back quite a way in the record of this government. The resolution reads as follows:

June 9, 1976

Whereas on May 14th, 1970, the Hon. Jean-Luc Pepin, Minister, Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, tabled a document known as the Canadian Textile Policy;
And whereas its intention was to give the textile trade in Canada-
That is referring to Mr. Pepin's document which he tabled.
-the necessary protection against low-cost and damaging offshore imports;
And whereas on the local scene there is much evidence of the Canadian textile industry being in serious trouble as evidenced by large lay-offs in two main fibre producing plants in this area and cut-backs in expansion of facilities and a slow down in production of output;
Now therefore the council of the county of Lennox and Addington requests the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce-
That is, the present minister.

to hasten the implementation of the immediate and long-term remedial action necessary to bring the textile trade in Canada to an acceptable economic level.
I also want to bring to the attention of the House and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Jamieson) that a major recommendation has been made to him by the Clothing and Textile Board with regard to polyester yarn and filament. It has been in his hands now for five weeks. The minister promised to table it in the House and to table his answer within 15 days. I ask the government, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, and the Prime Minister as well: In light of the serious situation now present in the general textile industry of Canada, why has this report not been tabled? Why has the minister failed to do this?
The Canadian economy at the present time is all tied up in knots, and the example I just gave is just one of the complaints. The Canadian economy is tied up in knots with the gold-dust twins, Jean-Luc Pepin and Beryl Plumptre, grinning and fawning as they try to justify their enormous salaries and preemptive power over every aspect of our economy. This is what the present government told Canadian voters in the 1974 federal election campaign could not possibly work. The Prime Minister was right, even as he was deceiving the voters into returning this government to office. Soon after the election, this government implemented a program of wage and price controls that had been drafted and approved long before the election campaign. The finance minister of that time has since resigned from the cabinet and from the House. There can be no doubt that the former minister knew a lot that we did not know, and do not know to this day, and that it was too much for him to accept and to live with and remain in the government.
We could have been less honest with the voters at that time, but that is not Conservative policy. We could have warned the people what to expect in the way of controls and restrictions if the then government were returned. Instead, we proposed a program-a sensible program-of selective income and price restraints, tied in with restraints in federal government spending-I repeat, tied in with restraints in federal government spending. The result of that honesty is history. The Prime Minister conned the Canadian voters and they turned down our sensible and reasonable restraints program. Now they are
The Budget-Mr. Alkenbrack
caught up in a gigantic and expensive bureaucratic web, and it is both possible and probable that our economy may never fully recover from the effects of these controls and restrictions.
I am surprised that the Minister of Finance did not use this opportunity to respond to the report of the Commissioner of Official Languages and slash the budget for bilingualism in the public service, since Mr. Spicer says it is a failure. We could find the money to buy the equipment and airplanes we need for our armed forces simply by establishing realistic priorities for government spending. The billion dollars we need for aircraft to replace the aging Argus patrol aircraft has been available to us, but most of it has been spent on bilingualism-"squandered" would be a better word.
What do we have for that money? We have a level of inefficiency in our public service that is lower than at any time in our history. There is no merit system left. We have a morale problem both in the public service and in our armed forces that is a disgrace. Our country is divided as never before in our history, yet we are told continually that bilingualism is bringing our people closer together. The plain fact is that this government's bilingualism program is destroying confederation by creating the two nations that the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) has been warning against for the past decade.
This would be a good time for the Minister of Finance to come clean on the ill-starred Lockheed deal, a boondoggle that threatens our good relations with our NATO partners and could cost us up to $20 million for nothing. The Minister of Supply and Services has found a likely goat to hang the Lockheed fiasco on, a public service official who cannot defend himself. The minister claims that he was not kept informed of what was going on in the Lockheed negotiations, so the offending official must go. What a travesty, Mr. Speaker!
I simply cannot believe that a minister of the Crown, a minister responsible for federal government purchasing, could suggest that he was not kept informed of negotiations on the largest proposed armed forces purchase in the history of our country. Even though we have seen the ultimate in inefficiency and bungling among cabinet ministers in this government, I still cannot accept the minister's statement that he did not make an attempt to follow each and every step in the Lockheed negotiations. If he allowed other people to carry out negotiations on their own, without assuming responsibility for what was said and done, then he cannot do anything except resign his cabinet post. Passing the buck to someone in the ranks is simply not good enough. It would not be acceptable on the part of a public servant, and it is not good enough for a minister of the Crown. What we need more than anything else, though, at this point in time is the full story of the Lockheed deal.
If it is true that a senior official in the public service is responsible for the colossal blunder that promises to cost the Canadian taxpayer $16 million or more, then we should know exactly how it happened so that we can plug that loophole. If a senior public servant has been guilty of negligence, or has been guilty of assuming authority to disburse sums from the treasury that were not lawfully his

June 9, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Alkenbrack
to assume authority for, then his indictment must be supported by facts, not innuendo, and this evidence must be presented to this House. The members on this side of the House who moved for a public inquiry are to be commended.
If, on the other hand, this is simply more ministerial bungling, then that minister must be forced to accept responsibility for the expenditure and in fact the misapplication of millions of dollars of public funds. For the minister to simply announce that he has fired an offending public service employee is not sufficient, Mr. Speaker, and the minister is not naive enough to believe that we will accept that as a full and complete explanation and expiation of this appalling example of negligence. This House, and through us the Canadian people, must be made aware of the full and complete story of the Lockheed affair.
Mr. Speaker, this might be the time and place to ask why the Prime Minister does not see fit to give us the full story on another case of ministerial shenanigans-the case of the Sky Shops contract tendering. My colleague, the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) has done a great service to all Canadians by exposing the sordid details of the Sky Shops affair and I do not intend to add to or detract from that member's excellent efforts. I only wish to say that there must be some compelling reason why the Prime Minister insists on protecting those involved in the Sky Shops affair, in a conspiracy of prime ministerial silence. I cannot help but wonder, Mr. Speaker, if one or more of the principals in that sordid affair might have been among the anonymous donors of the Prime Minister's now famous swimming pool. Could that be the reason for his reluctance to have the full story known?
There is one item in the budget that I concur with, and that is the provision to extend the eligibility period of insured employment from eight to twelve weeks in order to receive Unemployment Insurance Commission benefits. I do not agree with all its ramifications, but I agree with the time limit. This is not a sufficient reason to bring in a budget, though, Mr. Speaker. This could, and should, have been done long ago by the simple expedient of tabling a bill in the House. There is one thing wrong with this item, though, and that is the effect that it could have on people in areas of high unemployment, such as in the maritimes. Some of the traditional jobs in the maritimes, largely in fisheries, have a seasonal duration of eight weeks and these people will not now be eligible for benefits.
I urge the government to re-examine this provision in the UIC regulations to see if there is some way that these people can be considered as exceptions to this rule-not fishermen only, but others as well. I know that exceptions lead to more exceptions, but these are worthy exceptions. I know there is a danger that the desirable effects of this change in the regulations could be watered down, but surely we should be able to work out some way whereby these people will not be further penalized by a situation that is unique to the region or area in which they live. They might well become victims of the very uniqueness of their types of principal employment.
I have also suggested that if a way cannot be found to include them in the benefit program, then these people should not be required to pay unemployment insurance premiums in the first eight weeks. It would be grossly
unfair to expect anyone excluded from the benefit program to pay premiums. This principle is a sound one and it is in fact enshrined in the founding principles of the American revolution. The colonies, rightfully, refused to pay taxes to support a parliament in which they were not represented and could not therefore derive any benefit. This is a parallel to the question I have raised. I say that where there is no possibility of receiving benefits, there should not be the requirement to pay premiums.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having listened to the hon. member for Fron-tenac-Lennox and Addington (Mr. Alkenbrack) and heard him often refer to the budget as a "nothing" budget, I might conclude he made a "nothing" speech. I promise to read it tomorrow and appraise it fairly.

Mr. Speaker, the participation in this debate on the budget in the last few days is perhaps a repetition of some remarks already made. For some hon. members, it was congratulations to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), for other hon. members, it was an opportunity to speak on a topic, and for my hon. colleagues opposite, it was simply criticism, even negative criticism, because I heard nobody offer alternative solutions or even one alternative to the budgetary measures. In any case, I congratulate them for their participation in this democratic process.
I should like to join my colleagues who spoke before me to congratulate the Minister of Finance for his first budget. As the Canadian public on the whole seems to welcome it, and even if our most ardent critics from the media agree to say that this budget is trying to meet the needs of the state and of the economy at this time, it seems to me that perhaps the most important sector of our economy has been neglected namely agriculture.
It seems to me that there would have been room in the budget for these 5 or 6 per cent of the Canadian people who provide us with all our food. I will come back to this later. Even though I make this remark, Mr. Speaker, I must, in all sincerity, comend the Minister of Finance for several items of his budget.
First, concerning the conservation of energy, I fully endorse the proposed measures, namely the increases in the prices of oil and natural gas, so that the exploration and development of these resources may continue. Those who venture into that field assume enormous financial risks. It is very easy to criticize oil and multinational companies, but even if for economic reasons these companies decided to discontinue their research and exploration activities, we would be the first to feel the secondary effects of that decision. We would immediately be subject to the world price for oil, which would mean increases of almost 50 per cent, and I am convinced that this is not the wish of the Canadian people.
In my opinion, a price increase such as that proposed in the budget is a positive factor of conservation. We must realize that our per capita spending of non-renewable energy is higher than that of any other industrial country. It is a moral issue. We have no right to use more than our share of these non-renewable resources. We must leave

June 9, 1976

their fair share to the coming generations. A price increase would therefore bring the desired effect, that is less waste.
In his comments my hon. friend from York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) accuses this government of taking an overly large share of the tax on a gallon of gas-almost 13 cents. But he does not dare mention much higher taxes collected by provincial governments and particularly the producing provinces. At least that 10-cent federal tax is only aimed at protecting the consumers in the east of the country and if the hon. member for York-Simcoe wishes a return to the Borden line system he should have the honesty to admit it.
I wish also to mention the proposed changes to the unemployment insurance system. Merging unemployment insurance and manpower services is certainly a step in the right direction as those two services have so many things in common. The qualifying period will be increased from 8 to 12 weeks, a change which also received strong support because, in fact, the 8 weeks were mainly for the underprivileged areas which only have seasonal employment. But like in any good program there are abuses and changes must be made. We had reached the point where full employment areas had so many profiteers who worked only 8 weeks to qualify and received their benefits when in the same areas employers were looking for manpower. Then, I endorse those changes in principle but I shall encourage the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) to bring about all those changes to help areas with seasonal employment and to adopt even stricter measures for full employment areas.
For the less privileged areas maybe we should have LIP projects on a continuous basis but strictly with the cooperation of municipalities. We could even return to our Opportunities for Youth Program but still strictly with the cooperation of municipalities. It would eliminate criticism that some of those projects were not productive. There would be an authority or I should say a control.
Without any doubt, several of those projects gave very good results in our communities but as in the case of the 8-week qualifying period for unemployment insurance there were abuses. I was listening to my friend, the hon. member for York-Simcoe when he criticized the changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act. He asked that the unemployment insurance system operate on the principle that we should collect as much as we contribute. But two lines further he says that he supports the principle that the government should give a revenue to those who need it.

The hon. gentleman cannot have it both ways. He either supports a social measure, or he does not. This is something like his criticizing the government's policy on the Olympic gold coin which is being minted to help cover the Olympic deficit. He managed to slip the subject into his speech to show his refusal to co-operate on any measure concerning the Olympic deficit. Yet while he says this in the House, his leader, the hon. member for Rocky Mountain (Mr. Clark), is touring Quebec and telling the people of the province that if a Progressive Conservative government were to assume power in Ottawa, it would help the province directly to eliminate the Olympic deficit. Here, again, they cannot have it both ways. Inside Quebec they support the Olympics; outside Quebec they do not support them.
The Budget-Mr. Ethier
