speechtext:
In that budget closely following the antiinflation program, it is fair and reasonable to expect stricter measures concerning government expenditures. This means a sacrifice for a number of our citizens, because the reduction of government expenditures directly affects the social welfare programs directly or indirectly under our jurisdiction.
The changes to the unemployment insurance scheme will require sacrifices from the residents of areas where employment is seasonal. Urban dwellers are also asked to co-operate since the anti-inflation program is in effect. Many young unionists have seen their collective bargainings rejected by the Anti-Inflation Board. However, they had expected a raise comparable with what they had received in the last five years, which does not seem exaggerated. Professionals will have to restrict their increase in income to a limit of $2,400. Businesses will surely be asked to accept a smaller margin of profit.
The people in rural areas were also prepared to do their share. They were ready to make a sacrifice just as the rest of our society, but a shared sacrifice and not one supported only by the dairy community.
This is the main reason for my intervening today. Following the demonstration of June 3, it is obvious that there is a problem, an uneasy feeling, but we cannot and should not accept this responsibility alone. I have been quite surprised that so few producers understand the responsibility of their own marketing committee since this committee is composed of their own fellow producers who, as a matter of fact, appoint their delegates to sit on the management and supply committee with the Canadian Dairy Board.
I have been amazed and humiliated, Mr. Speaker, to see how the delegation treated the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) on June 3. I am sure several of the participants will regret this gesture, because they will soon find out how quickly they have forgotten their hero of the day before. Yes, I do say hero, for never in the history of Canada has a Minister of Agriculture done so much and in such a short time for those he is defending in cabinet.
Mr. Speaker, I would rather believe what many people have suggested, namely that this demonstration which was supposed to be peaceful turned out differently as a result of the infiltration of a few professional trouble makers. The large majority of producers are blaming the federal government for all the problems that the dairy industry is facing as a result. But the marketing boards have a responsibility and I would say it is their duty to better control the dairy production for 1975-76. They have done just the opposite. They have encouraged overproduction up to the very last minute. These marketing boards are operating under a provincial legislation so as to control production.
14338

June 9, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Ethier
That is why I say we will never agree to assume full responsibility.
As regards the problem which dairy producers are facing, at the beginning of the 1975-76 dairy year, the Minister of Agriculture informed the marketing boards through the Canadian Dairy Commission that the money available for subsidies amounted to only $266 million, that is $2.66 per hundred weight of milk. Obviously they meant that all production in excess of 100 million hundredweights of milk would not be subsidized.
In August and September 1975, the Canadian Dairy Commission and the Minister of Agriculture warned the producers and the marketing boards in particular that there was overproduction and that if this was not under control as soon as possible, it might have an adverse effect on the dairy industry especially in the industrial sector.
I read an article in the Ottawa Journal of May 8, 1976 where Ontario Agriculture Minister William Newman is quoted as still arguing that there is no overproduction in Ontario. Mr. Speaker, it is shameful for a minister to play on words in such a way. He knows very well the difference between production eligible for subsidies and quota production. True, the production has not gone over the quota but the minister should show a minimum of integrity and confess that our production was more important than what was necessary to be eligible for the subsidies and this is precisely where the problem is, namely the lack of money. The necessary production to be eligible for subsidies was 100 million hundredweights of milk and we have produced 112.6 million hundredweights. If we wanted to play with words, it would be very easy to say that we are not asking for a 5 per cent reduction but simply for a 15 per cent reduction, because last year we were asking for a production of 100 million hundredweights of milk and, this year, we ask for 95 million hundredweights to be eligible. But we do not want to play with words and we will not. There is a problem which must be dealt with, but before all we must be frank.
The problem is all the more important in Quebec because in that province there are two marketing bodies. The Federation of Industrial Milk Producers controls industrial milk producers and the Federation of Milk Producers controls producers of fluid milk and also the integrated producers, those who produce both fluid and industrial milk. I think that, here again, there is some misunderstanding. They too refused to assume their responsibilities and keep production below the necessary level to be eligible for subsidies. Here again, these two bodies are run according to a provincial law.
I think we are far from having a national policy with a single market for milk if, in one single province, they insist on keeping two federations, one for fluid milk and the other for industrial milk. I think that it would be more profitable to take some time to solve this problem of the two markets than to come and pour milk on Parliament hill.
Mr. Speaker, here are some propositions which might help this group which belongs to the industrial sector.
The cabinet could perhaps consider the possibility of creating a system to promote our dairy products on the export markets, at competitive prices. There might result a

lower price for our dairy products but not necessarily a reduction of net incomes. For example, with regard to the producer who is getting nothing for the milk produced in excess of his quota, I am sure he would choose to get a lower price, but for his whole production.
It will now cost the producer something for having overproduced, for not only will he not be paid anything for the excess milk but under the existing policy the Canadian Dairy Commission could charge the producer for a product he has not been paid for.
So a good advertising at world level is imperative if we are to find outlets for our dairy products, even at the risk of products commanding lower prices. If, as I was saying earlier, producers were free to produce as much as they want, this would have a double impact: higher income for producers and lower prices for consumers.
I would like to make another suggestion, Mr. Speaker. We could perhaps urge provincial governments to get back to the old custom of distributing free milk in primary schools and providing milk at special or reduced price in secondary schools. Schools should even be forced to have automatic vending machines for milk; there are always some for soft drinks, but seldom for milk.
I would like to make another suggestion if I may. There is still this agreement between producers and the Canadian Dairy Commission about the levy, that famous levy which affects industrial milk producers only. It is intended to cover the deficit incurred by the lower export prices compared with the home-market price or the subsidized price. This five year old agreement ought to be renegotiated and the burden could be shared in one of the two following ways: Either by the industrial milk producer, the natural milk producer, the processing plants and the two levels of government which are also responsible to the producers, or by the provincial and federal governments.
This would help us dispose of our present surpluses and empty out our storage rooms, then we could use the same system which is being practised in the European Economic Community, namely do away with the levy and, as I have said before, do away also with the export support price as the common market countries do.
Right now, our producers find themselves in competition with the government of those countries and not with the producers and I think this is not fair.
Another suggestion would be to have a single market for the milk but there again, as I said previously, as long as we insist on having two federations in one province, that does not seem possible.

I was pleased to read in today's Montreal Gazette that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) informed the producers that a two-year moratorium had been offered on the repayment of loans to the Farm Credit Corporation. I hope this will also include the interest. If not, it means very little to the producers who have just contracted large loans, since during the first years very little is in the form of repayment of capital; it is mostly interest.
Another welcomed announcement by the Minister was that the present limit of 95 million hundredweight will be raised if farmers demonstrate their willingness to stay within their assigned quota level. As I have said, there is a
June 9, 1976

serious problem for the industrial milk producers, and all those responsible should work together toward a policy or formula whereby situations such as the one we are not witnessing do not happen again. All those responsible should include the federal government, the provincial governments, the transformation plants, the fluid milk producers and the industrial milk producers.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this budget has been called a status quo or stand-pat budget by some. By others it is referred to in over-all terms as being fiscally neutral, a "wait and see" budget. That means we must wait and see if the American economy, slowly making its way out of its deep recession, will accelerate enough during the presidential election year to also lift our national economy by its bootstraps.
The budget, in essence, expects that the growth of the American economy will greatly improve the performance of our export sector. It seems to expect, at the same time, an increase of imports at reduced prices and thus improve our internal price structure as measured by the gross national product price deflater to 9.5 per cent. It projects a growth rate of 5 per cent which in real gross national product will just create enough new jobs to cover the increase in the labour force and thus leave us with average national unemployment that will remain at a seasonally adjusted rate of 7 per cent.
One of the disconcerting things about the budget, as I read it, is the finance minister's remark about the relationship between the present economic systems of control as characterized by the Anti-Inflation Board and what the economists call aggregate demand in the economy during peacetime conditions. He says on this point:
A clear lesson of history is that controls cannot be made to work in peacetime in the face of excess pressures of demand.
There is scarcely anyone who would argue the point, but surely even a neophyte Minister of Finance can see that when you have a seasonally adjusted 7.3 per cent level of national unemployment, you do not have an "excess demand" situation but a lack of demand. It surely called for some tax cuts or tax credits for the low income groups in this country. This lack of demand tends to create a level of unemployment which is about the highest in the western world. Indeed, if we exclude the United States we can truthfully say that Canada has by far the highest rate of unemployment in the western world.
Some would like to deny the reality of what that means in billions of dollars in goods and services which are not produced and which quantitatively and/or qualitatively could improve the lives of many Canadians. These people also think that young adults and women workers, with their material needs and desire for work, can be dismissed by trite slogans or phrases such as "marginal attachment to the labour force" or "secondary workers". The very people who measure their own standard of living by the level of their family income would deny that the same criterion be applied to hundreds of thousands of unemployed Canadians.
The old bromide is still around, that there are lots of job vacancies if "they" would only look. The fact is, Mr. Speak-
The Budget-Mr. Hogan
er, that we now have estimates from Statistics Canada on job vacancies which include both full and part-time categories. As the leader of our party noted earlier in this debate, these figures show there are now 12 unemployed Canadians for every available job in this country. He stated:
If every available job was filled tomorrow, there would be more than
700.000	Canadians who would be unable to find work.
The finance minister's remarks in the budget on Canada's central bank money supply growth targets provide clear evidence that a relatively tight money supply and an accompanying high structure of interest rates will be with us well into the future. The effect of this on our already overvalued exchange rate and the current account of our balance of payments-to say nothing of our own housing sector and investment in the business sector-and the likely consequent increase of unemployment is not seriously considered in this budget.
One may rightfully doubt that even a sluggish growth rate at this time, of 5 per cent, one which will produce
250.000	jobs and leave us with a 7 per cent level of national unemployment, will result from this so-called fiscally neutral budget. What if the game plan turns out to give us only 4 per cent or 4V4 per cent real growth in GNP? It will take at least six months fiscally to stimulate the economy back to a more stable and acceptable condition. Recent Economic history in Canada seems to suggest that it takes about $800 to $900 million to reduce the unemployment rate by about one percentage point.
Mr. Speaker, this budget does nothing of substance to fight unemployment. In fact, in my opinion it may increase it. It talks about productivity, but does little or nothing about it. It does nothing to reduce Canada's increasingly high interest rates. It is altogether too dependent on the economic stimulus of the American economy. It might be considered a fiscally neutral budget in over-all terms, but in reality it is more of a do-nothing budget. It certainly will not be neutral in its effect on certain sub-regions and categories of people who can least protect themselves.
Granted, single parent families and families in which both parents work will be able to make larger income tax deductions with respect to child-care expenses. The most significant change is in the proposed amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. Unemployment rates were recently at a 15-year high. What does the government do? Does it implement measures to stimulate employment? No. It makes it harder for those same unemployed people to receive benefits. This, despite the protestations of the Minister of Manpower (Mr. Andras), smacks of a cynical move on the part of the government to shift the blame of its failure to create jobs on to the very people who have suffered from that failure. On budget night the minister announced his intention to increase the number of weeks of insured employment from 8 to 12 with respect to eligibility for benefit. Regional extended benefits, he stated, would be related in a more sensitive manner to levels of regional unemployment. This second statement was taken as a concession to ease the burden of changes in areas of high unemployment. The Canadian Press story in the Halifax Herald of May 26 fell for this line when it stated:
This will result in a longer benefit period in areas of high unemployment such as the Atlantic provinces.
95 5 70-V/2

June 9, 1976
The Budget-Mr. Hogan
Mr. Speaker, I suggest this is not the case at all. Take, for example, a person who has worked for 12 weeks before losing his job, in a region with 10.5 per cent unemployment. At present, due to a system of national and regional extended benefits he could draw unemployment insurance for 44 weeks. Under the revised, and supposedly more sensitive system, he could collect for only 32 weeks. So much for helping the regions where unemployment is traditionally high!
I want to pursue this question of regional extended benefits. The minister claims they will be related in a more sensitive manner in future to levels of regional unemployment. The present legislation includes the notion of extension of benefits based on regional figures. The problem here is that the region chosen is, for example, the whole of the province of Nova Scotia. Let me show how this discriminates against the unemployed in Cape Breton, including my own constituency, that of Cape Breton-East Richmond, as well as that of Cape Breton-The Sydneys, Cape Breton Highland-Canso and other Nova Scotian ridings. Indeed, it applies to many ridings in the Atlantic provinces and probably through Quebec as well.
Under the normal labour force surveys carried out by Statistics Canada, Nova Scotia is divided into three economic zones for the purpose of measuring unemployment. Group four consists of the four counties on Cape Breton Island. Group five includes the eight counties from the Strait of Canso to the Bay of Fundy. Group six comprises Halifax County including the well-off Halifax-Dartmouth metropolitan area and the South Shore counties. The average unemployment rate in these three groups varied widely for 1975. Group four-Cape Breton Island-had 13 per cent unemployment. Group five had 7.5 unemployment. Group six experienced 6.2 per cent unemployment. But the unemployment rate for Nova Scotia as a whole was 7.8 per cent for 1975.
The Minister of Manpower and Immigration last Tuesday, I think it was, when he made his speech claimed that almost half of those who were in the category of the eight weeks are under the age of 25 and many are working wives and young persons living at home. What he left unsaid was that over half are over 25; 75,000 are between 25 and 34;
41,000	are between 35 and 44; 35,000 are between 45 and 54; and 19,000 are between 55 and 64. As for the charge that some of these people represent only a second income to the family, according to the 1971 census 6,200 heads of households in my riding draw less than $5,800. These families, surely, should not be denied a second source of income by the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Manpower and Immigration.
Further, the minister said that only 30 per cent of the 8 to 11-weekers have established a seasonal repeat pattern. That is only 110,000 Canadians in the course of a year. That is 110,000 people who quite probably will not even be able to remain where they are to work those 8 to 11 weeks per year if this measure passes. Has the minister given any thought to what will happen to these seasonal enterprises if the people can no longer stay in the area to work for the two months because it does not provide the necessary stamps to carry the person over the winter? Job creation is the proposed solution to the gap left by these measures.

suggest this is a sham. In reality it will be just replenishing the slashed coffers of LIP. LIP programs were cut in the last Turner budget, and now in reinstating some of the cut money the government tries to present this as a solution to high unemployment regions.
We will probably wind up making jobs for a couple of months so that people will be eligible to collect unemployment insurance benefits under the new qualification period. What does the Conservative manpower critic, the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), have to say about this mutilation of a fine piece of social legislation? Five years too late, he says, and he brags about amendments proposed by himself in 1971 to increase the insured period from 8 to 12 weeks. It is easy to see that the hon. member for Hamilton West does not have to live with serious structural and seasonal unemployment in his constituency. He may feel that people in his riding work for eight weeks, quit and draw pogey and then get another job. In many areas of this country the possibility of another job is just not there. I suggest the hon. member should listen to some of his maritime colleagues on this subject.
I want to return again to the question of unemployment regional figures and to show that under the present legislation the definition of "region", when it includes the whole of the province and does not include the sub-regions which are used in a labour survey conducted by Statistics Canada, completely discriminates against those areas of very high unemployment. In other words, in the example I gave previously, the fact that you have such low levels of unemployment, from 3 per cent to 4 per cent in the Halifax-Dartmouth region-which is part of region six-lowers the average level of unemployment, and therefore the extension of regional benefits to areas like Cape Breton Island is away down and we are getting gored in two ways. First, we are not getting the jobs, and we are not getting the compensation we should get because of the lack of jobs. As I mentioned in the example of Cape Breton Island, it has the worst of both worlds. It has the highest unemployment in the province, yet it is included with the Halifax-Dartmouth region which has had full employment, or much less than 6.2 per cent.
Under the proposed changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration has not given any indication that they plan to change the definition of "region" and, therefore, the basis for regional benefits. All the minister has to do to make the benefits more sensitive to the region is to follow the sub-regional patterns of unemployment that Statistics Canada already uses for its labour force survey. Regional benefits were designed to help areas with high unemployment, and Cape Breton, among others, is not being given its fair share of benefits. To repeat, our ox is being gored twice, as it were: first, in being forced to put up with intolerable rates of unemployment, and then in not getting fair compensation for the people suffering from these hardships.
By such devious statistical sleight-of-hand, this government gets out from under the moral and legal obligations accepted when the act was changed in 1971 to protect the unemployed who sincerely could not get work. God knows, we have battled long and hard for government policies to be designed to give them permanent employment, and we know from living with these people that 80 per cent to 85
June 9, 1976

per cent of them would be glad to have a job. This is particularly disturbing when we see that a recent study published by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, "Climate for Regional Development", which was published a few months ago, purported to show that during the 1970s economic progress, as measured by per capita national income, has increased in the Atlantic region in general.
It is even more optimistic about DREE's work in the Atlantic provinces, for it shows a pretty graph that reveals that even earned income per capita has increased for the Atlantic provinces. Alas for the DREE study. Mr. Andre Raynauld, the head of the Economic Council of Canada, said before the Standing Committee on Regional Economic Expansion that any increase in income levels in the Atlantic provinces vis-a-vis the rest of Canadian provinces is the result of transfer payments. It can also be documented from Statistics Canada that unemployment in the Atlantic area has increased since the inception of the anti-inflation, restraint program.
However, this study done by DREE showed that in Nova Scotia, for example, the disparity between the central core, that is, Halifax-Dartmouth and the peripheral area, including the whole of Cape Breton-with some 160,000 people- and southwestern Nova Scotia, advanced from 31 per cent to 37 per cent during the 1970s. When you consider that the 1971 census showed that Sydney, the only city in Cape Breton, had a per capita income that was only 68 per cent of the Canadian average, this is a disturbing trend. Glace Bay, the largest town in my constituency, was then only 54 per cent of the national average, and New Waterford, the next largest town, was only 48 per cent.
Little wonder that the former national Progressive Conservative party leader, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield), recently was quoted as telling a dinner meeting of the Dartmouth Chamber of Commerce, as quoted in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald., the following:
The disparities within our region have become just as great as those between our region and central Canada.
What is equally true for New Brunswick is more true for Newfoundland, and just as true to a large extent for Prince Edward Island. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) said that the Minister of Manpower and Immigration would have more to say on the matter. Did the Minister of Manpower use the occasion of his speech during the budget debate to enlighten us? The said fact is, so far as I am concerned after reading his speech, that we have to say "No." Is this government actively pursuing a policy that is linked to the concept of full employment? No. The minister says:
Our goal is the fullest employment rate possible, in light of inflationary pressures and the international economic situation.	.
These two qualifications are being used as an excuse for inaction. The Minister of Manpower quotes the Economic Council of Canada, but he does not heed their comments in regard to the Unemployment Insurance Act. The ECC's study, "People and Jobs", on page 39 says-and I hope all Liberals will listen to this:
We believe that most Canadians affected by unemployment are well served by the unemployment insurance system and use it honestly ... It would of course be possible to try to eliminate abuses by cutting certain
The Budget-Mr. Hogan
categories of claimants or the duration of benefits, or by extending the period of work, before claimants could become eligible for benefits. But such recommendations could prove harmful to persons most exposed to periodic and genuinely involuntary unemployment.
The report by the Economic Council of Canada recognized not only the fact that most Canadians use the program honestly, but also that it provided transfer payments to persons most exposed to uncertain or seasonal jobs. Unemployment insurance serves as a major income-stabilizing element in the economy, safeguarding purchasing power at crucial times for groups and areas that would otherwise suffer. This safeguard, I fear, is about to be knocked down for these groups and areas when they most need it.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, I would like to talk about what these proposed changes could mean for my area. According to our local Manpower centre, which I might add is most helpful in providing needed information, there are 11,000, out of a work force of 44,000, unemployed in industrial Cape Breton. This represents 25 per cent unemployment. That does not include student summer unemployment. The record of this government, as we see the unemployment situation across the nation at this time of year, especially among students, is absolutely abysmal. The government is waiting until next fall to come up with a program.
Our local economy is on the ropes and the government is about to provide a series of damaging body blows. The fishermen and fish plant workers, all seasonally employed, now have the added worry of not having enough stamps to collect unemployment insurance if it is a bad season. Even if they get 12, 15 or 20 weeks' work, the period for which they will be able to draw will be substantially reduced.
The Minister of Manpower and Immigration has not been truthful with parliament with regard to this matter. What will happen to the steelworkers laid off with no hope of being recalled until well into 1977? The Minister of Manpower-cynically, it seems to me-tries to argue that the figure of 330,000 individuals who would be affected by the increased eligibility requirement is wrong. He suggest that 100,000 at any one time would be affected. This is akin to the general who denies he had 12,000 troops die in a year, but says it was more like 1,000 a month. He states that almost half are under the age of 25 and many are working wives and young persons living at home. What is left unsaid is that over half are over 25. Furthermore, the minister says that only 80 per cent of the 8 to 11-weekers have established a seasonal repeat pattern. That is only
110,000	Canadians in the course of a year. There are 110,000 people who quite probably will not even be able to remain where they are to work those 8 to 11 weeks per year, if this measure passes.
I noted in passing what the manpower critic for the official opposition had to say in respect of minimizing the action of the government. In fact, if I may say so, the financial critic for the official opposition and the Minister of Manpower and Immigration seemed to be vying with one another as to who should receive the credit and who suggested this thing. The financial critic for the official opposition, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), congratulated the minister for adopting such a sound measure. During a question period after the budget I made up a little doggerel as I listened to the Minister of

June 9, 1976
Patent Medicines and Trade Marks Manpower and Immigration, the hon. member for Hamilton West and the hon. member for York-Simcoe vying concerning who should get the honour on this occasion. It goes like this:
Where could Mr. Andras have gotten An idea so stinky,
Likely from Cafik and Liberal Ontario Colleagues who are blinky,
But also of course from those vaunted Ontario Tories called sinkie and linkie.
The Tory manpower critic quotes editorials from the Globe and Mail to support his stand. He should also read the columnist on the same page. Geoff Stevens, in dealing with the budget, pointed out that tampering with the UIC legislation might gain the Liberals a few votes, but it would be a mean and crass political manoeuvre to hurt those in society who can defend themselves least. The member for Hamilton West is concerned about abuses and disincentives to work. Perhaps when he wants to quote editorials he should read the regional press. An editorial in the Cape Breton Post stated:
Finance minister Donald Macdonald estimates that about half of these workers will simply find work for the additional four weeks now required and thus will retain their eligibility. This estimate seems overly optimistic but, even assuming Mr. Macdonald is correct, the implication is that those workers only stay on a job long enough to qualify for the pogey.
In effect, they are shirkers who would rather collect UIC benefits than go to work. Yet they are the ones who will retain their eligibility. At worst, they will be inconvenienced by having to work an extra month.
It is the other half of these 330,000 citizens (or more than half, if our guess is correct), those who are genuinely incapable of finding steady employment, who will suffer in Cape Breton, during the present economic travail.

subtopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT, AND TRADE MARKS ACT MEASURE TO EXTEND LICENCE DATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I would be remiss in my position as health critic for the official opposition if I did not make a few comments at this stage on the bill. I am sorry that the parliamentary secre-

tary and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) both think it is of little importance and neither of them is here, having known well in advance that it would be coming up at this time.
We gave this bill a fairly careful look in committee and we learned a couple of things. I think the position which we took earlier in refusing to let it whistle through the House at all stages in one sitting, without any questions asked or any debate, was justified. We have seen examples that there has been a good deal of shortsightedness on the part of the government, and even a little bullheadedness when they dealt with this matter when it was presented to the House in the form of Bill S-9.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the bill deals with the repeal of the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act and replaces it with certain regulations under the Food and Drugs Act, provision 10, part C of the food and drug regulations. When this matter was first before the Senate, the Proprietary Association of Canada stated that they would require a December 31, 1976, proclamation date in order to have sufficient time to make changes in labelling and packaging to conform with this legislation. For some reason, the government at that time adopted a stubborn position and insisted on moving the date up to July 1, 1976. Very shortly thereafter it became obvious to the Proprietary Association of Canada, as well as to the government, that the representations made by that association in the first place were valid and that the date would have to be moved forward. So here we are, once again dealing with a bill which, if it had been carefully studied in the first place, and if the government had paid the slightest attention to the results of its consultations with the industry involved, we would not have before us now.
One of the reasons given, which struck me as rather strange, was that the principal hold-up which made it impossible for the industry to be ready for July 1 was the government itself because of its failure to provide certain numbers to its proprietary patent medicines, which are required in order that the labels be appropriately printed. When we were before the committee there was another show of gross sloppiness on the part of the government in that they had the parliamentary secretary speak on behalf of the government, but no officials of any sort. Indeed, there was nobody there to answer any questions on behalf of the government. The parliamentary secretary took a few guesses, but in the final analysis we had Mr. Don Harper, the president of the Proprietary Association of Canada, giving answers on behalf of the government.
Here was a man representing private industry answering questions in committee and trying to explain things on behalf of the government whose representatives were unable to provide us with the information required. I think that is a rather shameful approach by this government to parliament and to the committee system. It indicates a certain disregard, perhaps even a certain disrespect, for the validity of the work that committees do, because if the government had had regard for our committee's work it would have at least provided us with some experts or civil servants who could give us answers to questions.
We will not hold up this bill. As a matter of fact, we agree with its intent and we think it is necessary. We agree with the bill on the basis of assurances given us in written
June 9, 1976

form that the provinces will be ready to comply with this legislation by April 1, 1977. We agree with it, also, on the basis of assurances given us by the Proprietary Association of Canada that they will be ready on April 1 with their new labels and packaging.
With those few comments, I will conclude my remarks. Let me say, Mr. Speaker, that if anybody from the government side is listening-which I doubt-I hope they will have learned a lesson from this experience which suggests that if the job is not done right the first time, it has to be done again and in the long run this wastes everybody's time. We on this side of the House are not interested in wasting anybody's time. We think the government has a responsibility to try to run its business in an efficient
Patent Medicines and Trade Marks
manner, but in my view the manner in which this bill has been dealt with is far from efficient.
